lessons.title: Power BI Fundamentals
lessons.description: The Power BI workflow: Get Data, Transform, Model, Visualise, Share.
lessons.theory_md:
## Power BI Fundamentals

### Why Power BI, when you already know SQL and Excel?
You already know how to query data (SQL) and calculate with it (Excel). Power BI's job is different: it turns that data into something a decision-maker can explore themselves, interactively, without ever writing a query — and it does this at a scale Excel starts to struggle with (millions of rows, live-connected to a database).

### The three tools that make up Power BI
- **Power BI Desktop** — where you build. Free, installed on your PC. Everything below happens here.
- **Power BI Service** — the browser-based home for publishing and sharing what you built.
- **Power BI Mobile** — a phone/tablet app for viewing published reports on the go.

You build in Desktop, publish to Service, view anywhere.

### The five-stage workflow — the shape of every project
1. **Get Data** — connect to Excel files, SQL databases, web APIs, folders of CSVs, and dozens of other sources.
2. **Power Query** — clean and reshape the raw data (covered in depth next lesson). This is the same *idea* as Excel's Power Query, and if you've cleaned data in pandas, the transforms will feel familiar too.
3. **Data Model** — define how your tables relate to each other (covered in "Data Modelling & Relationships"). This is conceptually identical to the JOIN logic you already know from SQL — you're just drawing it visually instead of writing `ON a.id = b.id`.
4. **Report View** — build the actual charts, tables, and interactive elements business users will click through.
5. **Publish** — push the finished report to Power BI Service so others can access it without needing Desktop installed.

### Your first look at the interface
When you open Power BI Desktop, three icons on the left sidebar matter most:
- **Report view** (the default) — your visual canvas, page by page.
- **Data view** — inspect the actual rows in each loaded table, like a read-only spreadsheet.
- **Model view** — see and edit the relationships between your tables.

### Why this workflow order matters
Doing these steps out of order is the single most common cause of a frustrating Power BI experience. Cleaning data in Power Query *before* modelling saves you from building relationships on messy columns. Building the model *before* the report saves you from re-doing visuals every time you fix a relationship. Follow the order above, in that order, every time.

**Business context:** A sales director who can't write SQL should still be able to open a Power BI report, click "North Region," and instantly see every chart update. That self-serve exploration — with zero risk of them ever seeing or breaking the underlying query — is the entire value proposition of this tool.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: the Get Data -> Data Model -> Report workflow mirrors how you'd query (SELECT), then join (JOIN), then present results - same pipeline, visual instead of code.
- **Excel**: if you've used Power Query or PivotTables in Excel, the underlying engine here is genuinely the same one, just in a dedicated tool built for it.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between a Power BI 'dataset' and a 'report'?
options: They are the same thing with two names
A dataset is the underlying data model; a report is the visual layer built on top of it
A report contains the raw data; a dataset contains only charts
Datasets are for Excel, reports are for Power BI
quiz.explanation: The dataset is your data model (tables, relationships, measures); the report is the visuals built to explore and present that model - one dataset can support many different reports.

quiz.question: Which Power BI tool would you use to clean and reshape messy data before it enters your model?
quiz.explanation: Power Query is where transformations happen - splitting columns, removing duplicates, fixing types - all before the data ever reaches your model.

quiz.question: What is DAX primarily used for in Power BI?
options: Writing calculations and measures against your data model
quiz.explanation: DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language for building measures and calculated columns - it is to Power BI what formulas are to Excel.

lessons.title: DAX Basics
lessons.description: Calculated columns, measures and the most useful DAX functions.
lessons.theory_md:
## DAX Basics — Data Analysis Expressions

### The formula language of Power BI
DAX is to Power BI what formulas are to Excel — the language you use to calculate anything beyond what's already in your raw data. If you've written an Excel formula, DAX's syntax will feel familiar; if you've written a SQL aggregate function like `SUM()` or `AVG()`, the underlying concepts will feel very familiar too.

### Measures vs. Calculated Columns — the most important distinction to get right early
| | Measure | Calculated Column |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluated | At query/interaction time | Once, at data refresh |
| Responds to | Filter context (slicers, clicks) | Row context only |
| Storage | Not stored — calculated live | Stored in the model, taking up memory |

**Rule of thumb:** if the calculation should change as a user clicks a slicer (e.g. "Total Sales" that updates when they filter to North region), it's a measure. If it's a fixed value per row that doesn't depend on what's filtered (e.g. a "Full Name" column combining first + last name), it's a calculated column.

### Essential functions to know first
```dax
SUM(table[column])              -- total a column
AVERAGE(table[column])          -- same idea as SQL's AVG()
COUNTROWS(table)                -- row count, like SQL's COUNT(*)
CALCULATE(expression, filter)   -- re-evaluate an expression under a different filter — covered fully next lesson
DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, [alternate_result])  -- division that won't crash on divide-by-zero
RELATED(table[column])          -- pull a value across a relationship, like a JOIN would in SQL
```

### Your first real measure
```dax
Total Revenue = SUM(FactBilling[bill_amount])
Average Bill = AVERAGE(FactBilling[bill_amount])
Bill Count = COUNTROWS(FactBilling)
```
Create these by right-clicking a table → **New Measure**, then typing the formula. Once created, drag the measure onto any visual — it will automatically recalculate as the user filters the report.

### Why DIVIDE instead of the `/` operator
```dax
Margin % = DIVIDE([Profit], [Revenue])
```
If Revenue happens to be zero for some filter combination, `/` throws a visible error in your report. `DIVIDE` returns blank (or a value you specify) instead — always prefer it over a raw division symbol.

**Business context:** The exact same "average bill amount" you'd calculate with `AVG(bill_amount)` in SQL, or `AVERAGE()` in Excel, or `df['bill_amount'].mean()` in pandas — is `AVERAGE(FactBilling[bill_amount])` here. Four tools, one concept, four syntaxes. Once you notice this pattern, learning each new tool gets faster.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: SUM(), AVERAGE(), COUNTROWS() are DAX's versions of SQL's SUM(), AVG(), COUNT() - same aggregation concepts, different syntax.
- **Excel**: DAX measures play the same role Excel formulas do - calculating something beyond what's in the raw data.

lessons.title: Data Modelling & Relationships
lessons.description: Build a star schema model that connects your tables correctly.
lessons.theory_md:
## Data Modelling & Relationships

### The model is the foundation — get this wrong and everything after is harder
The model determines what you're even able to calculate. A badly structured model makes every DAX formula a fight; a well-structured one makes most formulas almost write themselves. This is worth slowing down for.

### Star schema — the standard shape
- **Fact table** — the large table of transactions or events (e.g. every hospital bill, every sale). Has foreign keys pointing outward.
- **Dimension tables** — smaller lookup tables describing *who, what, where, when* (e.g. a table of patients, a table of dates, a table of products). Each has a primary key.

```
DimDate ──── FactSales ──── DimProduct
                │
            DimCustomer
```

If this looks familiar, it should — it's the exact same relational structure you already learned in SQL's JOIN lesson. A `FactSales` table full of foreign keys joining out to smaller dimension tables *is* what you were writing `INNER JOIN ... ON` statements against. Power BI just draws the relationship instead of you typing it every query.

### Creating a relationship
In **Model view**, drag a field from one table onto the matching field in another. Power BI detects the cardinality automatically in most cases:
- Primary key (unique values) → foreign key (repeating values) = **one-to-many** ✓ — this is the relationship type you want in almost every real model.
- Many-to-many relationships are usually a sign the model needs restructuring, not a feature to reach for casually.

### Cardinality reference
| Setting | When to use |
|---|---|
| One-to-many | The standard fact-to-dimension relationship |
| One-to-one | Splitting one logical table into two for readability |
| Many-to-many | Bridge tables, or "role-playing" dimensions used more than once |

### Cross-filter direction — the setting that causes the most confusion
- **Single** (the default, and almost always correct) — filters flow from the dimension table to the fact table. Click "North" on a region slicer, and every fact-table visual filters accordingly.
- **Both** — filters flow in both directions. This can produce results that look wrong (ambiguous filtering) if used without understanding exactly why. Reach for Single first; only switch to Both when you have a specific, well-understood reason to.

**Business context:** Exactly the same hospital patients/billing relationship you queried with `JOIN` in SQL — one patient, many bills — is the relationship you'd model here as one-to-many between DimPatients and FactBilling. The logic never changes across tools; only the syntax does.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **SQL**: a relationship here is exactly what a JOIN is in SQL - Power BI just draws the connection instead of writing ON a.id = b.id.
- **Excel**: this replaces the need for most VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP formulas once your model is built correctly.

lessons.title: Advanced DAX
lessons.description: CALCULATE, FILTER, time intelligence, and the measures that make Power BI powerful.
lessons.theory_md:
## Advanced DAX

### CALCULATE — the single most important function in DAX
`CALCULATE` re-evaluates an expression under a modified filter — it's the mechanism behind almost every non-trivial DAX measure you'll ever write.
```dax
Sales YTD = CALCULATE(
    SUM(FactSales[Revenue]),
    DATESYTD(DimDate[Date])
)

Sales North = CALCULATE(
    [Total Revenue],
    DimRegion[Region] = "North"
)
```
Read the second example as: *"Take the Total Revenue measure, but force the filter to only 'North', regardless of whatever the user has actually clicked."* This is how you build a fixed comparison point (e.g. "vs North") that sits alongside whatever the user is currently filtering to.

### Time Intelligence — comparing across time periods
This requires a proper Date table, explicitly marked as one (**Table tools → Mark as Date Table**) — Power BI's time functions depend on this to work correctly.
```dax
Revenue LY = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))
Revenue MoM % = DIVIDE([Total Revenue] - [Revenue LM], [Revenue LM])
```
`SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` shifts the current filter back exactly one year — the same comparison a financial analyst does manually in Excel by referencing last year's column, just automatic and correct regardless of which period the user is currently viewing.

### Variables — making complex DAX readable
```dax
Revenue Growth =
VAR CurrentRev = [Total Revenue]
VAR LastYearRev = [Revenue LY]
RETURN DIVIDE(CurrentRev - LastYearRev, LastYearRev, 0)
```
Without variables, this same formula would need to repeat the `[Total Revenue]` and `[Revenue LY]` calculations inline, twice, making it both harder to read and slower to calculate (DAX would otherwise compute each measure reference separately). `VAR` computes each once, then reuses the result — always prefer this pattern once a formula has more than one moving part.

### A worked example, start to finish
Say you want "this month's revenue vs. the same month last year, as a percentage":
```dax
Revenue = SUM(FactBilling[bill_amount])

Revenue LY =
CALCULATE([Revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))

Revenue YoY % =
VAR Current = [Revenue]
VAR Prior = [Revenue LY]
RETURN DIVIDE(Current - Prior, Prior, BLANK())
```
Each measure builds on the one before it — this layering (simple measure → time-shifted version → comparison) is the standard pattern for almost every real KPI you'll build.

**Business context:** "Are we up or down versus this time last year?" is one of the three most common questions any manager asks of any report. `CALCULATE` + `SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR` is how you answer it correctly, automatically, for every single filter combination a user might click into.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Statistics**: the Time Series lesson's trend and moving-average concepts are exactly what CALCULATE + time intelligence functions implement here.
- **Business**: year-over-year comparisons built here are usually the exact KPI a stakeholder presentation leads with.

lessons.title: Power Query in Power BI
lessons.description: Clean and shape data before it hits the model — the right place to fix messy data.
lessons.theory_md:
## Power Query in Power BI

### Same tool, same job as Excel — bigger stage
If you completed Excel's Power Query lesson, almost everything here will feel familiar — it's genuinely the same engine under the hood. The difference is scale: Power BI's Power Query routinely handles millions of rows pulled live from a database, not a few thousand rows in a workbook.

### Where cleaning belongs: before the model, not after
Transform data in Power Query (**Get Data → Transform Data**), never in DAX. This is a rule, not a preference: Power Query transformations run once, at refresh time. DAX measures recalculate on every single click a user makes in the report. Doing cleanup work in DAX means paying that computational cost over and over, forever — cleaning it once in Power Query is dramatically more efficient.

### Applied Steps — your undo-able recipe
Every transform you apply appears as a step in the **Applied Steps** panel on the right, in order. Click any earlier step to see exactly what the data looked like at that point — this makes Power Query far safer to experiment in than it looks; nothing is destructive until you click Close & Apply.

### The essential transforms
```
Remove Duplicates → ensures one row per key (e.g. one row per patient_id)
Replace Values    → fix typos: "Online " → "Online"
Split Column      → "John Smith" → "John" | "Smith"
Pivot / Unpivot   → reshape wide-format data to long, or long to wide
Merge Queries     → the visual equivalent of a SQL JOIN — combine two tables on a matching column
Append Queries    → the visual equivalent of a SQL UNION — stack two tables with the same columns
Group By          → aggregate rows, like SQL's GROUP BY
```
If you know SQL, every single one of these has a direct one-to-one equivalent you already understand — Power Query just does it with clicks instead of syntax.

### Writing your own transform: the M language
Power Query records every click as M code behind the scenes. You can also write custom columns directly:
```
= [Revenue] - [Cost]
= Date.Year([OrderDate])
= Text.Upper([ProductName])
```
This is the same logic as an Excel formula or a Python calculated column — same idea, different syntax.

### Incremental Refresh — for genuinely large tables
Once a table reaches millions of rows, reloading the *entire* table on every refresh becomes slow and wasteful. Incremental Refresh lets you set a date range parameter so Power BI only reloads new or changed rows going forward, not the whole history every time.

**Business context:** A finance team refreshing a 5-million-row transactions table every morning at 6am needs this to finish before the workday starts — incremental refresh is often the difference between a report that's ready on time and one that isn't.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Excel**: this is the exact same Power Query engine as Excel's - everything transfers directly, just operating at a larger scale here.
- **SQL**: Merge Queries and Group By are Power Query's point-and-click equivalents of JOIN and GROUP BY.

lessons.title: Report Design & UX
lessons.description: Build reports people actually use — layout, colour, and interaction patterns.
lessons.theory_md:
## Report Design & UX

### The 5-second rule
A business user should understand the main message of a report page within 5 seconds of looking at it — before reading a single label. If they can't, the page has too much competing for attention, or nothing is actually prioritized.

### Layout — the Z-pattern
Eyes naturally scan in a Z: top-left → top-right → bottom-left → bottom-right. Use this:
- **Top-left**: the single most important KPI card.
- **Top-right**: the primary trend chart (context for that KPI over time).
- **Bottom-left**: a breakdown (by region, by category — whatever explains *why*).
- **Bottom-right**: supporting detail.

Align every visual to a grid (**View → Snap to Grid**) — misaligned visuals are one of the fastest ways a report reads as unpolished, even when the data itself is solid.

### Colour — restraint is the skill
- Pick **one accent colour** for the metric that matters most on a page. Everything else should be a neutral grey.
- Colouring every visual a different colour looks decorative, not informative — it actively works against the 5-second rule.
- Reserve red/green specifically for conditional formatting (below/above target) — don't also use red/green decoratively elsewhere, or the meaning gets diluted.

### Slicers vs. Filters — a distinction worth getting right
- **Slicers** are visible on the canvas — the user sees and controls them directly. Use these for exploration you *want* the user doing themselves (e.g. "pick your region").
- **The Filters pane** applies a constraint invisibly — the user never sees or changes it. Use this for things you, the report builder, need fixed (e.g. "only show active accounts").

### Tooltips and Bookmarks — the two features that make a report feel "built," not just "assembled"
- A custom **tooltip page** (Page → Page type → Tooltip) shows rich detail on hover, without permanently cluttering the main canvas with every possible number.
- **Bookmarks** (View → Bookmarks) save a specific filter state, which you can then wire to a button — letting a user click "By Region" vs "By Product" and instantly reconfigure the whole page without touching a single slicer.

**Business context:** The same report, with good layout and restrained colour, gets used daily. The same data with a cluttered, rainbow-coloured, misaligned layout gets opened once and never again — design quality directly determines whether analytical work actually gets used.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Excel**: the Dashboard Design lesson's layout and colour principles apply directly here, just in a more interactive canvas.
- **Business**: the Data Storytelling lesson's "lead with the insight" principle is what should drive every layout decision on this page.

lessons.title: Publishing & Sharing
lessons.description: Publish to Power BI Service, manage workspaces, and set up scheduled refresh.
lessons.theory_md:
## Publishing & Sharing

### From Desktop to the world: Publish
**Home → Publish → select a workspace.** This uploads your report (and the dataset behind it) to Power BI Service, where others can access it through a browser — no Desktop installation required on their end.

### The vocabulary of Power BI Service
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Workspace | A shared folder/team space — where reports and datasets live together |
| Dataset | The data model — separate from any report built on top of it |
| Report | The visual layer — the pages and charts a viewer actually sees |
| Dashboard | A single page of pinned tiles pulled from one or more reports |
| App | A packaged, polished version of a workspace, published for end-users who should never see the underlying build |

One dataset can support several different reports — this is exactly why keeping the model (Lesson: Data Modelling) clean matters even after you've built your first report; you're not starting over for the next one.

### Scheduled Refresh — keeping published data current
Once published, the report is a snapshot until you configure refresh:
1. Dataset settings → **Data source credentials** → sign in so the Service can reach the original source.
2. **Scheduled refresh** → set a frequency (up to 48 times a day on Premium capacity, 8 times a day on Pro).

### Sharing options, and when to use each
- **Share a report** — grants access to specific named users or security groups. The default, safest choice for anything containing real business data.
- **Publish to web** — generates a public URL with no login required. ⚠️ Never use this for anything containing real customer, financial, or employee data — anyone with the link can view it, forever, with no audit trail.
- **Embed** — puts the report inside SharePoint, Teams, or a custom web application, respecting the same permissions as Power BI itself.
- **Power BI App** — the cleanest option for a polished, end-user-facing deployment; it hides the workspace's internal structure entirely.

### Row-Level Security (RLS) — one report, personalized per viewer
```dax
[Region] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
```
Set this in Desktop (**Modelling → Manage Roles**), test it locally with **View as Role**, then assign real users to that role once published in Service. The result: every regional manager opens the exact same report and dashboard, but each only ever sees their own region's data — one build, personalized automatically per viewer.

**Business context:** This is the payoff for everything in this module — a report built once, modelled correctly, refreshed automatically, and shared securely to exactly the right audience, each seeing only what they're supposed to. That's the difference between a one-off analysis and a real production reporting system.

## 🔗 How This Connects
- **Business**: the Stakeholder Presentations lesson's delivery considerations (who sees what, how it's revisited later) are exactly what Sharing and Row-Level Security solve here technically.

exercises.title: Dataset vs Report
exercises.prompt: You update the underlying data in your SQL database. After refreshing the Power BI dataset, do you need to republish the report?
exercises.hint_1: The report is separate from the dataset.
exercises.hint_2: Refresh updates the dataset; the report reads from the dataset.
exercises.hint_3: No — refreshing the dataset updates the data. The report automatically reflects the new data without republishing.

exercises.title: Publish to web risk
exercises.prompt: A colleague asks you to use Publish to Web for a report containing employee salaries. Should you? Why?
exercises.hint_1: Think about who can access a public URL.
exercises.hint_2: Anyone with the URL can see the data.
exercises.hint_3: No — Publish to Web creates a public URL accessible to anyone, which is inappropriate for sensitive data like employee salaries. Use share or embed with authentication instead.
